summary:
California fire activity, 2000 to today

Problem. NASA's two fire sensors count differently. MODIS (since 2000) uses 1 km pixels. VIIRS (since 2012) uses 375 m pixels and picks up about 4.4x more detections. So you can't directly compare today's fires to the 2000s.

What we built. One fire record for California, 2000 to today, in VIIRS units. The whole site runs on it.

How.
1. Merge VIIRS pixels. VIIRS detections in the same 1 km square on the same pass count as one fire. That drops VIIRS from 4.4x MODIS to 2.3x. This is our "true VIIRS".
2. Predict VIIRS before 2012. A model trained on 2012 onward learns what VIIRS would see from what MODIS saw, then fills in 2000-2011.
3. Test it fairly. Each year is predicted by a model that never saw it. Monthly predictions are off by a factor of about 1.17, and the 90% range holds 90% of test months.

Data. NASA FIRMS detections sampled 15 days a month (741,675 total), plus US Forest Service named fires up to 2020, 42 of them linked to Wikipedia.

The Explorer (app/). Pick a region and dates on the map. You get summary tiles, a chart of MODIS, VIIRS and the prediction, recorded fires, fire season, and the harmonization steps for your area (4.36x to 2.33x to 0.93x). You can download a report, hotspots (CSV or GeoJSON) and a monthly CSV. The link reopens the exact view.


Limitations.
- Sampled data, so rates are per sampled day.
- Less accurate in small areas.
- Statewide, the prediction runs about 7% low.
details: Our project combines NASA's two fire-detecting satellite records, MODIS and VIIRS, into one consistent fire record for California from 2000 to today by merging VIIRS detections in the same 1 km square into one fire and training a model to predict what VIIRS would have seen before 2012. The benefit is a single record with an honest uncertainty range that you can explore on a map and download. The intended impact is letting researchers, fire agencies and the public tell whether today's fire activity is unusual compared with the 2000s. We built it with Python for the data pipeline and model, plain HTML for the web app, and data from NASA FIRMS, the US Forest Service and Wikipedia, with the code on GitHub. It is creative because instead of only scaling one satellite to match the other, we first fixed the reason they differ, which is one fire lighting up several small VIIRS pixels. We considered honest testing (no year is predicted by a model that saw it), the limits of sampled data, lower accuracy in small areas, and the fact that the prediction runs about 7% low statewide.
